title: The main classifications of assets and liabilities
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Classify the assets and liabilities a business holds into their main groups, using examples, and read those classifications on a statement of financial position.

blocks.heading: Assets: what the business owns
blocks.text: An asset is an item of value that a business owns and expects to use in its operations or turn into cash. Assets are sorted by how long the item is expected to stay. A non-current asset is kept for use for more than a year: the ovens and premises of a Windhoek bakery, a farmer's tractor, a delivery vehicle. A current asset is expected to be used, sold or turned into cash within a year: inventories such as flour waiting to be baked, trade receivables owed by credit customers, and cash itself. The same van shows the test: kept for deliveries it is a non-current asset; held for resale it is part of inventories.

blocks.heading: Liabilities: what the business owes
blocks.text: A liability is a debt the business owes to an outside person or business. Current liabilities fall due within a year: the trade payables owed to suppliers who sold on credit, wages owing at the end of the month, and a bank overdraft, which the bank may ask to be repaid at short notice. Non-current liabilities fall due after more than a year, most often a long-term bank loan repayable over several years. The one-year test that sorts assets sorts liabilities the same way, because debts paid soon need cash in the coming months, while a loan spread over years gives room to pay.

blocks.heading: Sorting items in practice
blocks.text: Keetmanshoop Tool Hire owns its workshop and a fleet of drills and ladders, holds fuel and spares for the coming weeks, is owed money by a builder who rented on credit, and owes money to its hardware supplier, on a five-year loan and on an overdraft. The workshop and fleet are non-current assets; the fuel, spares and the builder's debt are current assets; the supplier's invoice and the overdraft are current liabilities; the loan is a non-current liability. A bicycle repair shop in Copenhagen sorts the same way: its spanners are non-current assets, the inner tubes on its shelf are inventories.

blocks.text: Topic 5.2 shows how the timing of receivables and payables drives the cash-flow forecast. Topic 5.3 explains the income statement, which reports profit and costs over a period, while the classifications here describe one date. Topic 5.5 turns these figures into ratios that measure liquidity and performance.
